title: Secretary's Day

jokes.text: Oscar realizes she's been sitting on her Girl Scout cookies: 'Wait, I'm sitting on them. This is awesome.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is asked if she's seen the Girl Scout cookies Toby left on her chair
jokes.punchline: She discovers she's been sitting on them and her delighted reaction ('This is awesome') is absurdly cheerful given she's crushed her cookies
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean physical-comedy beat with an unexpectedly sunny reaction. The enthusiasm is the joke. Functional but not special.

jokes.text: Kevin's voicemail imitating Cookie Monster: 'What's the difference between a chimichanga, a chalupa and a tostada? Call me back ASAP. It's urgent.'
jokes.setup: Someone plays a voicemail Kevin left that parodies Cookie Monster's voice
jokes.punchline: The Cookie Monster voice is used to convey hilariously mundane food-related urgency — a chimichanga vs chalupa inquiry treated as a genuine emergency
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Kevin doing a Cookie Monster impression, and the content of the message being exactly what Kevin would consider urgent. The Mexican food taxonomy question treated as a crisis is perfect Kevin characterization. High character integration — only Kevin would ask this with this level of urgency.

jokes.text: Kevin protests the impression: 'Wait, this isn't funny. I don't talk like that.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has just heard his own Cookie Monster-esque voicemail played back to the office
jokes.punchline: Kevin denies sounding like Cookie Monster despite the voicemail being clearly Cookie Monster-esque, with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Classic lack-of-self-awareness comedy well-suited to Kevin. The denial lands because the audience just heard the evidence. Competent but expected.

jokes.text: 'Say, "Me eat cookie." / No. I won't say it.'
jokes.setup: Someone tries to get Kevin to perform the Cookie Monster voice for the crowd
jokes.punchline: Kevin refuses with indignant dignity, which is inherently funny given his previous total lack of self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy escalation of the Kevin/Cookie Monster bit. His wounded dignity is funny but not especially sharp writing.

jokes.text: Michael sees the crowd: 'Why is everyone clumped around accounting? Break it up, you clique.'
jokes.setup: The office has gathered around accounting to watch the Cookie Monster video
jokes.punchline: Michael calls them a 'clique' with an offended tone, as if gathering to watch a funny video is an act of social exclusion against him
jokes.explanation: Michael's insecure need to be included manifests as hostility toward anyone having fun without him. Consistent character work, though not a standout line.

jokes.text: Michael on Sesame Street: 'Is that the program where all those puppets live in the barrio?'
jokes.setup: Someone identifies Sesame Street to Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael's description of Sesame Street as 'puppets in the barrio' is both technically somewhat accurate and completely tone-deaf, revealing he barely knows what Sesame Street is
jokes.explanation: 'The barrio' is a hilariously reductive but not entirely wrong description of Sesame Street's setting. It reveals Michael's cultural obliviousness while also being inadvertently accurate. Strong Michael characterization — only he would describe it this way with complete sincerity.

jokes.text: Michael watches the Kevin/Cookie Monster video: 'This is Kevin. This is Kevin.' Then: 'Thank you. That is an amusing link. I'd like it sent to me, please.'
jokes.setup: Michael just told everyone to break it up, implying he disapproves
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately asks for the link to be sent to him, completely undermining his own authority
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael self-contradiction — posturing authority then immediately abandoning it to participate in the thing he just banned. The formal language ('amusing link') makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Angela objects: 'This is inappropriate.' / Michael: 'This is my favorite day.'
jokes.setup: Angela tries to shut down the video-watching with a moral objection
jokes.punchline: Michael's gleeful counter — 'This is my favorite day' — completely dismisses her while also being a disproportionate response to watching a funny video
jokes.explanation: Good economy — Angela's stiff propriety vs. Michael's childlike joy compressed into two short lines. The hyperbole ('my favorite day') for something this minor is well-calibrated Michael behavior.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'It is Erin's and my three-week anniversary, so perfect storm for a romantic gesture.'
jokes.setup: Andy explains it's Secretary's Day
jokes.punchline: He describes a three-week anniversary as a 'perfect storm' worthy of a romantic gesture, revealing his over-investment in a very new relationship
jokes.explanation: Andy's romantic over-eagerness is established quickly and efficiently. 'Three-week anniversary' as a 'perfect storm' is a nice absurdist touch that characterizes him well without being surprising.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional: 'I sent an email blast, a text blast, a good old-fashioned talk blast... I sent a snail-mail blast a week ago, and a stern reminder via fax at 7:00 this morning, so people better step up and appreciate the crap out of Erin.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants the office to remember Secretary's Day
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of communication methods — including 'snail-mail blast' sent a week in advance — reveals obsessive, manic energy that culminates in 'appreciate the crap out of Erin'
jokes.explanation: The escalating list is well-constructed — each item is funnier than the last. 'Snail-mail blast' is a great oxymoron. 'Appreciate the crap out of' is a satisfying culminating absurdity. Good structure.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional: 'If it wasn't for secretaries, I wouldn't have a stepmom.'
jokes.setup: Michael is reflecting on Secretary's Day
jokes.punchline: He reveals his father had an affair with his secretary, which became his stepmother — stated with complete casual pride rather than trauma
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Extraordinary economy — one sentence reveals a dysfunctional family backstory, Michael's obliviousness to social norms, and his weirdly positive spin on objectively problematic situations. The casual delivery of what would devastate most people is peak Michael Scott. The line is highly quotable and recontextualizes Secretary's Day in a darkly funny way.

jokes.text: Pam's confessional on maternity leave: 'It rocked. It rocked my ass off.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Pam what maternity leave was like, expecting a nuanced answer
jokes.punchline: Pam delivers an extremely enthusiastic but comically vulgar and inarticulate response — 'rocked my ass off' — that's at odds with her typical warm/measured demeanor
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the contrast between the setup (thoughtful question) and the aggressively casual answer. Works well as a character beat showing Pam's relief at being back and her refreshed bluntness after leave. Not a top-tier joke but very functional.

jokes.text: Pam discovers her dead plant: 'Oh. You couldn't have watered it? / I literally did not know that existed until this moment.' / Dwight: 'Well, I knew it existed, and I chose to let it die.'
jokes.setup: Pam returns from maternity leave and discovers her desk plant is dead
jokes.punchline: The coworker admits ignorance, then Dwight escalates by confessing he deliberately let it die — stated with Dwight's signature cold conviction
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure works beautifully: ignorance followed by deliberate malice. Dwight's matter-of-fact admission that he chose to let it die is perfectly in character — he has a farmer's unsentimental relationship with life and death. The escalation from 'didn't know' to 'chose to kill' is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Michael describes Erin: 'She's kind of a rube.' / Andy: 'That's my girlfriend you're talking about.'
jokes.setup: Pam is convincing Michael to take Erin to lunch for Secretary's Day; Michael is reluctant
jokes.punchline: Michael's blunt assessment ('she's kind of a rube') delivered without any awareness that he's insulting Andy's girlfriend — and Andy's mild defense makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Michael's oblivious rudeness is well-deployed. The word 'rube' feels authentic to Michael's self-aggrandizing vocabulary. The exchange is efficient and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Erin to Michael: 'I got a picture of you asking me to lunch.'
jokes.setup: Michael formally asks Erin to lunch
jokes.punchline: Erin's response that she 'got a picture' of him asking is bizarre and non-sequitur — implying she mentally photographed the moment as something precious, which is both sweet and very odd
jokes.explanation: Erin's peculiar folk idiom ('got a picture of you') is a great character detail — it feels like something someone who grew up in an unusual environment would say. It's strange, endearing, and original. High character integration because this phrasing is distinctly Erin.

jokes.text: Erin critiques Michael's lunch suggestion: 'Well, Hayworth's is more business-casual, and they always screw up your order...' / Michael: 'Oh. Yeah, okay. Yeah, that was a stupid suggestion.'
jokes.setup: Michael suggests Hayworth's as a special restaurant
jokes.punchline: Erin immediately and bluntly dismisses it on multiple grounds, and Michael instantly folds and agrees it was 'stupid' — showing his total lack of confidence when challenged
jokes.explanation: Functional beat showing Erin's unintentional social bluntness and Michael's fragility. Not particularly original but serves the character dynamics efficiently.

jokes.text: The pair ultimately goes to Hayworth's anyway: 'Okay, let's go to Hayworth's.' / Erin: 'Okay!'
jokes.setup: Erin just finished dismissing Hayworth's as a bad choice
jokes.punchline: They end up going anyway with Erin's enthusiastic agreement, undermining her entire critique
jokes.explanation: A clean callback payoff — the restaurant critique comes to nothing. Light but effective. The joke is purely structural.

jokes.text: Kevin refuses a cookie from the tray: 'Yeah, ha, ha, tray of cookies. I'm not falling for that.' / Darryl: 'I brought those in. It's my birthday.'
jokes.setup: Someone offers Kevin cookies
jokes.punchline: Kevin assumes it's a Cookie Monster prank and refuses with sarcastic wisdom — but the cookies are genuine birthday cookies, making his paranoia both sad and funny
jokes.explanation: A satisfying reversal — Kevin's self-protective instinct backfires and he misses Darryl's birthday cookies entirely. The beat works because of the Cookie Monster running gag and also because Kevin's logic ('I'm not falling for that') is coherent but wrong. Good use of misdirection.

jokes.text: Kevin to Darryl after learning it's his birthday cookies: 'That's some stone-cold narcissism right there.'
jokes.setup: Darryl clarifies the cookies are birthday cookies he brought in himself
jokes.punchline: Kevin accuses Darryl of narcissism for bringing birthday cookies — the accusation is completely backwards and reveals Kevin's utter lack of social norms
jokes.explanation: Kevin's twisted logic — that bringing your own birthday cookies is narcissism — is wonderfully wrong and completely Kevin. The confidence of the accusation elevates it. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: 'They're making fun of Cookie Monster. I get that. But in a strange way, it feels like they're making fun of me.'
jokes.setup: Kevin reflects on the Cookie Monster video in a confessional
jokes.punchline: He can't quite put together why mocking Cookie Monster feels personal — the audience can, but Kevin genuinely can't — which is the joke
jokes.explanation: Kevin's complete lack of self-awareness is perfectly deployed here. He knows something is off but can't identify what. The phrase 'in a strange way' is exactly how someone with zero self-awareness would frame this moment of near-insight. High character integration — this is an all-time Kevin beat.

jokes.text: Kevin's confessional continues: 'Oscar, did you eat some of my M&M's? The level...' [trails off into unrelated grievance mid-self-reflection]
jokes.setup: Kevin is mid-confessional about his feelings on the Cookie Monster mockery
jokes.punchline: He abruptly pivots to accusing Oscar of eating his M&Ms, abandoning the introspective thread entirely
jokes.explanation: The interrupted confessional is a great structural gag — it's as if Kevin's attention simply drifted. The M&M grievance is perfectly mundane, and the 'The level...' trailing off suggests he was building up to something that never arrives. Pure Kevin.

jokes.text: Kevin watches more of the video: 'This is violent and offensive.' [pause] 'Thank you.' / 'And it really makes me self-conscious about my voice.' / 'That's awful.' / 'I'm not crying.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is watching the Cookie Monster parody video
jokes.punchline: His rapid-fire emotional responses — offense, gratitude, self-consciousness, denial of tears — cascade in a way that reveals he both hates and loves the attention
jokes.explanation: 'I'm not crying' as a punchline to a sequence of contradictory reactions is classic. 'Thank you' inserted between 'violent and offensive' is a great beat showing Kevin's complicated relationship with being the center of attention. Well-escalated.

jokes.text: Gabe's confessional: 'And some of them still think that I'm the IT guy.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is explaining the challenges of establishing authority as the new corporate liaison
jokes.punchline: His final grievance — being mistaken for IT — is anticlimactic but reveals he's even less visible than he thought
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke about Gabe's near-invisibility. The IT guy mix-up is a good specific detail. Functional but mild.

jokes.text: Gabe's confessional: 'This Cookie Monster thing is an opportunity to show people that I'm an authority figure.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is trying to establish authority at the Scranton office
jokes.punchline: He frames a viral office video about Cookie Monster as his big authority-proving moment — revealing how low the bar is for his leadership
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment for Gabe — his authority-proving ambitions are laughably small. The joke lies in the gap between his serious delivery and the trivial battlefield he's chosen.

jokes.text: Gabe's speech: 'It is now forbidden to talk, joke about, or email this around.' / 'Not to be scary, but yeah, I would listen to me.'
jokes.setup: Gabe addresses the office to ban the Cookie Monster video
jokes.punchline: 'Not to be scary, but yeah, I would listen to me' is the least intimidating threat imaginable — the qualifier 'not to be scary' already undermines any authority, and 'I would listen to me' is absurdly self-referential
jokes.explanation: Gabe's failed authority moment is beautifully written. 'Not to be scary, but...' is already an admission that he isn't scary. 'I would listen to me' is a weird, circular self-endorsement that highlights how little external validation he commands. High character specificity — this is a very Gabe sentence.

jokes.text: Michael asks to listen to book on tape in the car; Erin: 'This is a novelization of the movie Precious, Based on the Book Push by Sapphire.'
jokes.setup: Michael was hoping to have conversation on the drive to the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Erin wants to listen to the novelization of a movie (which is itself based on a novel) — a double-adaptation absurdity — and the full verbose title delivered seriously is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is layered: (1) the absurdity of a novelization of a movie, (2) the full pedantic title with full attribution, and (3) it being Erin's choice of light car entertainment. The title itself becomes a running gag later in the episode. Good setup for callbacks.

jokes.text: Michael's conversation attempt: 'What decade would you have chosen to be a teenager?' / Erin: 'I don't know.' / Michael: 'I would have chosen the 1490s. 'Cause America was discovered. Right.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to make conversation with Erin in the car
jokes.punchline: Michael's answer — the 1490s to be a teenager when 'America was discovered' — is historically bizarre (America was discovered by Columbus in 1492, and Michael would be choosing to be a teenager in late medieval Europe to witness something from afar) and delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Michael's answer reveals his shallow relationship with history — he wants to be there for 'American discovery' without thinking through what that means for a teenager in 1490s Europe. The breezy 'Right.' at the end, seeking validation from Erin, is a perfect Michael touch. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Erin's confessional: 'My last job was at a Taco Bell Express, but then it became a full Taco Bell and I don't know, I couldn't keep up.'
jokes.setup: Erin is sharing her work history
jokes.punchline: She was overwhelmed when Taco Bell Express upgraded to a full Taco Bell — the implication that a fuller menu was beyond her capacities is both sad and hilarious
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. The specificity of 'Taco Bell Express' vs 'full Taco Bell' is inspired — it's a real distinction that most people know exists. The idea that the upgrade overwhelmed her is devastating in its smallness. Erin delivering this without any awareness of how it sounds is perfect. 'I don't know, I couldn't keep up' is a beautifully underplayed punchline. This is original, character-specific, economical, and earned. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft.

jokes.text: Erin: 'My favorite part about being a receptionist is that I get to have my own desk. At my foster home I never had a desk.'
jokes.setup: Erin is sharing what she loves about her job
jokes.punchline: Her benchmark for professional fulfillment is owning a desk — contextually heartbreaking when we learn it's because she grew up in foster care without one
jokes.explanation: This joke operates in the space between comedy and pathos that The Office does best. The desk as the pinnacle of professional ambition is funny; the foster home context makes it poignant. The backpedaling ('I don't mean I didn't like my foster home. I did like it. I just didn't have a desk there.') is perfectly Erin — trying to be fair to people who may have failed her. Strong character writing.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I've been trying. I've been trying to keep it going.'
jokes.setup: Michael is struggling to maintain conversation with Erin, who has given very short answers
jokes.punchline: His defeated confessional about 'trying to keep it going' — said with genuine exhaustion — confirms that the drive was a conversational disaster
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat that confirms the social awkwardness we've been watching. Not especially original but serves the scene efficiently.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional: 'Erin is just weird. How many pillows do you sleep on at night?'
jokes.setup: Michael is critiquing Erin's conversational abilities after a failed car ride
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to asking Erin the extremely strange question 'how many pillows do you sleep on at night?' — which is offered as an example of good conversation but is itself bizarre
jokes.explanation: Michael calling Erin weird while his example of good conversation is 'how many pillows do you sleep on' is a great ironic inversion. The joke is that Michael's idea of normal conversation is itself strange, without him realizing it.

jokes.text: Erin's answer to the pillow question: 'Yeah, like a favorite month. Like, I liked April when I was seven.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Erin if she had a favorite age or month
jokes.punchline: Erin's answer — 'I liked April when I was seven' — is strangely specific and delivered as if it's a perfectly normal thing to say
jokes.explanation: Erin's answer is charmingly odd — the intersection of 'month' and 'age' she produces ('April when I was seven') is sweet and weird. Another piece of her character mosaic. Doesn't land as hard as her bigger bits but contributes to her comic portrait.

jokes.text: Michael describes Andy to Erin: 'Andy plays the banjo. Yeah, I love that. Other than the fact that he dated Angela, I don't think he is a snappy dresser.'
jokes.setup: Erin asks Michael to tell her about Andy before she met him
jokes.punchline: Michael sandwiches the bombshell ('he dated Angela') between banal character assessments (banjo, fashion) as if they're equivalent information — the casual delivery of major relationship news is the joke, and it detonates slowly
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's narrative pivot delivered as a comedy beat, and it's beautifully structured. Michael buries the devastating Angela revelation between two mundane Andy observations, treating it as equivalent information. The structure mirrors Michael's emotional intelligence — he has no idea what's important. The misdirection (we're focused on the banjo/fashion stuff) makes the Angela line land harder. Excellent craft.

jokes.text: Erin: 'Why wouldn't he tell me that?' / Michael: 'Probably didn't want you to have a mental image of him having sex with somebody else.' / Erin: 'They had sex?' / Michael: 'They were engaged, so...'
jokes.setup: Erin is reacting to learning Andy dated Angela
jokes.punchline: Michael's blunt 'mental image of sex' explanation opens a new wound (Erin didn't know they had sex), which Michael then escalates further ('they were engaged, so...') with each revelation worse than the last
jokes.explanation: Each line digs the hole deeper. Michael is obliviously helpful — he's trying to explain Erin's confusion but each explanation is more damaging. 'They were engaged, so...' trailing off is perfect: the implication completes itself. Classic escalation structure with strong character-specific delivery.

jokes.text: Erin: 'I asked for pickles on my burger, and there are only, like, five or six. Can I get some more pickles?' / Waiter: 'Of course. I'll get you a bowl of pickles.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of an emotional crisis (learning Andy was engaged to Angela), Erin interrupts to complain about pickle quantity
jokes.punchline: Erin's most urgent concern in this moment is getting more pickles — 'five or six' pickles isn't enough — which reveals her emotional coping mechanism (denial through mundanity)
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash — emotional crisis interrupted by pickle logistics — is a great cringe beat. 'Five or six' is specific enough to feel real. The waiter's unfazed 'I'll get you a bowl of pickles' is an inadvertently perfect response. The mundane overwhelming the emotional is a signature Office move.

jokes.text: Erin begins braiding/playing with her hair at the restaurant table in full public meltdown; Michael: 'What are you doing? What are you doing?' / Erin: 'In the foster home, my hair was my room.'
jokes.setup: Erin is processing the Angela revelation and appears to be dissociating — she starts doing something physical with her hair
jokes.punchline: 'In the foster home, my hair was my room' is both the saddest and funniest sentence — it's a non-explanation that explains everything about Erin while being completely bizarre
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best line and one of The Office's great one-liners. 'In the foster home, my hair was my room' is a perfect piece of comedy writing: it's deeply specific, completely original, character-defining, and lands with exactly the right mixture of heartbreak and absurdity. It tells us everything about Erin's childhood in seven words while being utterly inexplicable as practical information. The economy is extraordinary — it's simultaneously the funniest and saddest line in the episode. Comparable to the 9.5 anchor in concept, slightly below in quotability reach, but an elite joke.

jokes.text: Man at nearby restaurant table calls out: 'I'll have what she's having.'
jokes.setup: Erin is having a very public emotional meltdown at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: A stranger delivers the famous 'When Harry Met Sally' line, implying Erin's breakdown looks like the orgasm scene from that film — a meta movie reference that also reframes her breakdown as accidentally entertaining
jokes.explanation: The reference is instantly recognizable and the application is clever — Erin's emotional display being interpreted as the Sally orgasm scene works. However, it's a borrowed joke with low originality. The When Harry Met Sally callback is a well-worn comedic shortcut. Impact is decent because of audience recognition, but craft suffers for relying entirely on pre-existing material.

jokes.text: Michael returns from lunch and peppers Erin with anxious questions: 'Did you have a... Did you like your lunch? Did you have a good lunch? Did you like that? Did you enjoy your food?' / Erin: 'It was good. I liked my lunch.'
jokes.setup: Michael returns from what was clearly a disaster lunch with Erin
jokes.punchline: His rapid-fire, overlapping attempts to reassure himself that lunch was fine — six different phrasings of the same question — reveals his social anxiety, and Erin's flat 'It was good. I liked my lunch.' is deflating
jokes.explanation: The verbal flailing is recognizable Michael behavior. Erin's flat response is a good deadpan. The repetition works but goes slightly too long. Functional cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight on Pam's breast milk: 'Same thing happens with my cows if I don't tend them frequently enough. You gotta milk them, or else they'll moo like crazy.'
jokes.setup: The office discovers Pam is uncomfortable because her milk is coming in and she needs her breast pump
jokes.punchline: Dwight offers an agricultural parallel — comparing Pam to his cows — with complete earnestness, as if this is helpful medical advice
jokes.explanation: The cow comparison is both accurate (biologically parallel) and wildly inappropriate in context. Only Dwight would say this with helpful intent rather than cruelty. Strong character integration — the farming knowledge applied to human situations is a reliable Dwight formula.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Really? Fine. Let your breasts explode. Three squeezes and I would drain you.'
jokes.setup: Pam declines Dwight's offer to help and says she'll check the bathroom first
jokes.punchline: Dwight's wounded response — 'let your breasts explode' — and his confident claim about 'three squeezes' is grotesquely practical and completely oblivious to social norms
jokes.explanation: 'Let your breasts explode' as a parting shot is darkly funny — a consequence delivered as a mild threat. 'Three squeezes and I would drain you' is simultaneously gross and delivered with the confidence of a livestock professional. The absurd specificity ('three squeezes') elevates it.

jokes.text: Meredith is caught using Pam's breast pump: 'I just like the way it feels.' / Pam: 'Give it back to me, now!' / Meredith: 'I was just warming it up.' / Pam: 'That's... It's disgusting!' / Meredith: 'We're both girls. Who cares?'
jokes.setup: Pam can't find her breast pump
jokes.punchline: Meredith has been using it for personal pleasure — her defense ('I was just warming it up' / 'We're both girls. Who cares?') is both absurd and completely in character for Meredith
jokes.explanation: This is peak Meredith. Only she would use someone's breast pump for personal gratification and defend it with a shrug. 'We're both girls. Who cares?' is a genuinely funny line because its logic is so wrong but Meredith finds it totally sound. 'I was just warming it up' is an escalating defense that makes things worse. The sterility concern is the realistic kicker. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Andy asks about lunch: 'Was it everything that you hoped and dreamed it might be?'
jokes.setup: Andy eagerly asks Erin about the Secretary's Day lunch he arranged
jokes.punchline: His over-the-top phrasing ('hoped and dreamed') for what was a casual lunch reveals how much emotional investment he put into something that went catastrophically wrong
jokes.explanation: The dramatic phrasing foreshadows the disaster we're about to see. Functional character beat showing Andy's investment. Not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Erin snaps at Oscar during confrontation with Andy: 'God, Oscar, will you keep your pants on? It's easy.'
jokes.setup: Erin is in the middle of a tense standoff with Andy; Oscar asks about fax cover sheets
jokes.punchline: Erin's misdirected anger at Oscar (who asked an entirely innocent question) is absurd, and 'keep your pants on, it's easy' as a command is weirdly specific and off
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'keep your pants on' used in this context is a bit off — it usually means 'calm down' but Erin seems to be deploying it differently, which makes it funnier. Her anger displacement onto Oscar is a good beat. 'It's easy' as an add-on is strange and specific.

jokes.text: Kevin does the Cookie Monster impression in his confessional: 'My name is Kevin. I'm an accountant.' / Jim: 'It's a little derivative.' / Kevin: 'But parody is always derivative.'
jokes.setup: Kevin performs his Cookie Monster impression for the camera
jokes.punchline: Jim's critique ('a little derivative') is met by Kevin's surprisingly sophisticated defense ('parody is always derivative') — which is technically correct, making it funnier
jokes.explanation: Kevin accidentally making a correct critical theory argument is a great subversion of his established dimness. 'Parody is always derivative' is technically true and makes Jim look slightly foolish for the critique. The unexpected intelligence from Kevin is the joke.

jokes.text: Jim does Andy impression: 'Michael, can I have an advance on my paycheck, because a Mrs. Fields Cookies just opened up at the mall!'
jokes.setup: The group is doing impressions; Jim does Andy as Cookie Monster
jokes.punchline: Jim's Andy-as-Cookie-Monster is about cookies (appropriate) but the request — advance pay specifically for Mrs. Fields — is a perfect lampooning of Andy's aristocratic-but-desperate personality
jokes.explanation: The Mrs. Fields specificity is good — it's upscale-but-accessible, which fits Andy's personality. However, the impression bit overall doesn't reach the heights of the stronger Cookie Monster jokes.

jokes.text: Kevin does Gabe impression: 'Sorry, Gabe, but that show hasn't been on in many cookies.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is doing a Gabe impression while maintaining the Cookie Monster voice
jokes.punchline: 'Many cookies' substituted for 'many years' is a fusion of the Cookie Monster voice and Gabe's presumed reference to MADtv — the substitution is delightfully nonsensical
jokes.explanation: 'Hasn't been on in many cookies' is a clean, funny substitution. The Cookie Monster logic (replace abstract time with cookies) applied to Gabe's pretentious reference is a good layered joke. Efficient and well-timed.

jokes.text: Gabe interrupts the impressions: 'Okay. Hey, can I have your attention, please?' [then pivots to introduce the party and thank Angela]
jokes.setup: People are doing impressions of Gabe in front of him
jokes.punchline: Gabe's response to being mocked is to pretend it didn't happen and pivot to party logistics — his strategy for authority is to ignore challenges to it entirely
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is subtle — Gabe's non-response to being mocked is itself character comedy, but it's understated enough to not be a big laugh. Functional.

jokes.text: Gabe's attempt is called out as trying too hard: 'Why don't we leave the parodies to the pros at MADtv?' — another character passive-aggressively dismissing Gabe's attempt.
jokes.setup: Gabe contributes his own Kevin/Cookie Monster impression.
jokes.punchline: Being told to defer to MADtv — a show widely considered worse than SNL — as the gold standard for parody is a subtle insult.

jokes.text: Gabe praises Angela: 'A very special shout-out to the chair of the party planning committee, Miss Angela Martin. You have outdone yourself.' / Michael immediately: 'Yeah, you know what? I think we can all agree that Angela's not so great, so...'
jokes.setup: Gabe gives Angela a sincere compliment in front of the whole office
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately and aggressively contradicts the compliment — 'I think we can all agree that Angela's not so great' — with zero context or social awareness
jokes.explanation: Michael's reflexive need to contradict a compliment he didn't give is good character work. 'I think we can all agree' creating a false consensus is a very Michael rhetorical move. The correction from Gabe ('I'm saying the exact opposite') is a good straight-man beat.

jokes.text: Andy's speech about Erin: 'That 115-pound moonbeam over there named Erin Hannon... to a lot of you she may just be the person who brings you your fax confirmations, but to me, she is my girlfriend, in addition to being the person who brings me my fax confirmations.'
jokes.setup: Andy is giving a romantic speech about Erin at the Secretary's Day party
jokes.punchline: After the poetic 'moonbeam' opener, he undermines his own romantic declaration by noting she's also, practically, still just the person who brings him fax confirmations — putting the mundane task on equal footing with 'my girlfriend'
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'fax confirmations' at the end of an otherwise romantic speech is a well-structured joke. 'Moonbeam' as a descriptor for Erin is both charming and ridiculous. The structure (poetic → practical → poetic → practical again) works well.

jokes.text: Andy announces 'Secretary of Love' and begins playing banjo — then Erin immediately interrupts to confront him about Angela mid-performance.
jokes.setup: Andy launches into a romantic banjo serenade for Erin at the party, having just given a heartfelt speech
jokes.punchline: The serenade is immediately obliterated as Erin cuts in with 'I know about Angela' — the more elaborately romantic Andy made this moment, the more catastrophic the public destruction is
jokes.explanation: The structural comedy here is excellent — the episode has built to this moment through multiple setups (Andy's obsessive preparation, the Angela revelation at lunch). The banjo serenade setup maximizes the comedic impact of the interruption. The bigger the romantic gesture, the more devastating the public confrontation. The juxtaposition of banjo music starting and immediately being cut off is strong visual/audio comedy that would land hard in viewing.

jokes.text: Erin's public questioning of Andy: 'Did you sleep with Phyllis or Kelly or Pam? Maybe all together?'
jokes.setup: Erin is publicly confronting Andy about his romantic history
jokes.punchline: 'Maybe all together?' is an absurd escalation — Erin's mind has gone straight to the most extreme scenario, delivered with earnest panic rather than accusation
jokes.explanation: The escalation to group sex as a genuine fear (not a joke) is absurd and perfectly Erin. The inclusion of Pam specifically is a good detail — Pam is the most obviously implausible choice, which makes Erin's spiral more extreme. 'Maybe all together' lands well because it's delivered as genuine concern, not sarcasm.

jokes.text: The office responds to Erin's question 'Did everyone know? Was I the only one who didn't know?' with: 'Yeah. Pretty much.' / 'Pretty much. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Erin desperately asks if she was the only one who didn't know about Andy and Angela
jokes.punchline: The casual confirmation — 'Yeah. Pretty much.' with overlapping agreement — is both brutally honest and socially oblivious. The lack of any attempt to soften the blow is the joke
jokes.explanation: The group's breezy confirmation of Erin's worst fear is dark comedy done well. The multiple 'pretty much's piling up is a good cringe beat. The casualness of delivery is the comedy.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional: 'I should probably get involved in this, but I think my energy is better spent on the Cookie Monster issue.'
jokes.setup: A relationship crisis is exploding at the Secretary's Day party Michael organized
jokes.punchline: Michael has decided the Cookie Monster viral video is more important than the human crisis unfolding in front of him — the wrong prioritization is delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Michael's priority inversion is perfect — in his mind, managing his own minor embarrassment (the Cookie Monster video) outweighs the romantic crisis he helped cause. The confessional framing makes his obliviousness even sharper. Good callback integration.

jokes.text: Kevin does Michael impression: 'Hey, Erin, you look delicious! I mean, beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is apparently doing impressions at the party, now doing Michael
jokes.punchline: 'You look delicious! I mean, beautiful' — the slip from 'delicious' to 'beautiful' is a perfect Michael Scottism, capturing his oblivious sexual inappropriateness and fumbling correction
jokes.explanation: 'Delicious' as an unintentional compliment that Michael would then correct reveals Kevin has a good read on Michael's specific brand of HR violations. The self-correction ('I mean, beautiful') is accurate to Michael's character. A competent impression joke.

jokes.text: Michael 'suspends' Pam, then Jim, then Dwight for slow-clapping: 'Wait, what? I was just slow-clapping your no-nonsense decision-making.' / Michael: 'I don't want to hear it. Suspended.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to exercise authority by suspending Pam; Jim objects; then Dwight slow-claps in support of Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael suspends each person in sequence, including Dwight who was actively supporting him — the escalating absurdity culminates in punishing his own ally
jokes.explanation: The escalating suspensions are well-structured. Suspending Dwight for slow-clapping is the peak absurdity — Michael's power trip extends even to punishing support. The structure (suspend Pam → suspend Jim → suspend Dwight for defending Michael) escalates cleanly.

jokes.text: Kevin, after the suspension scene: '"C" is for suspension.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just issued a 'C is for...' style statement referencing Cookie Monster
jokes.punchline: Kevin co-opts the Cookie Monster 'C is for cookie' format to comment on the suspensions — 'C is for suspension' makes no literal sense (suspension starts with S) but Kevin delivers it with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Kevin's application of the 'C is for...' formula to a word that doesn't start with C is the joke — he's using the structure without understanding it. The confidence of the delivery and the wrongness of the logic is pure Kevin. One of the episode's best Cookie Monster gag payoffs. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Pam defends herself to Michael: 'Andy, she's not the easiest person in the world to have a conversation with... who doesn't tell their girlfriend that they were engaged to someone who works four feet away from them? That's like... That's... That's like Mr. & Mrs. Smith crap.'
jokes.setup: Pam is defending her role in revealing the Angela secret to Erin
jokes.punchline: 'That's like Mr. & Mrs. Smith crap' — comparing Andy and Angela's secret engagement to a spy thriller where Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie kill each other is an absurdly outsized pop culture reference for the situation
jokes.explanation: The Mr. & Mrs. Smith reference is slightly forced — the connection isn't quite tight enough to land hard. It's a mild laugh from the excess of the comparison. Pam's general argument is sound but the joke itself is weak.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional spiral: 'Who cares? I mean, it's not like I killed somebody. Big deal, right? This is gonna blow over in two seconds. She never asked me, so if you think about it, it's kind of... I probably should have told her, I guess. Everybody does stupid things.'
jokes.setup: Andy is doing a confessional where he tries to minimize his mistake
jokes.punchline: He begins with bravado ('who cares, it's not like I killed somebody') and within five seconds has arrived at contrition ('I probably should have told her, I guess') — the speed of the collapse is the joke
jokes.explanation: The rapid collapse from confidence to responsibility is a good Andy character beat. His emotional arc compressed into one confessional is well-structured. The 'if you think about it, it's kind of...' trailing off before the reversal is particularly good — he can't even complete the rationalization.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Everyone here knows that I can't and won't keep a secret.' [beat] — delivered with complete conviction as his defense for not being secretive
jokes.setup: Andy argues that he would never keep a secret from Erin
jokes.punchline: His proof of trustworthiness is that he's constitutionally incapable of secrecy — which is both untrue (he DID keep a secret) and not actually a virtue
jokes.explanation: The self-contradiction is good — Andy presents his inability to keep secrets as a defense while currently keeping one. The confident delivery of a clearly false self-assessment is classic Andy.

jokes.text: Andy's escalating self-talk: 'She never asked me, so if you think about it, it's kind of... I probably should have told her, I guess. Everybody does stupid things.'
jokes.setup: Andy is rationalizing in a talking head, cycling through defenses
jokes.punchline: He begins with a victim-blame ('she never asked'), retreats mid-sentence, then settles on 'everybody does stupid things' — the full collapse of his argument in 10 seconds
jokes.explanation: The micro-arc of Andy's self-justification collapsing in one talking head is excellent — the 'if you think about it, it's kind of...' trailing off is the structural key. He can't even finish his own bad argument. Good Andy character work.

jokes.text: Erin to Andy: 'You want to talk to me, come to my desk.' — delivered from across the room with maximum frost
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to approach Erin to reconcile
jokes.punchline: Erin weaponizes her desk — the one she loves so much because she never had one in the foster home — as a power position
jokes.explanation: Erin using her desk as a power position is a subtle callback that deepens the joke on rewatch. The cold delivery from someone usually warm is effective character contrast.

jokes.text: Angela to Erin at the fax machine: 'You embarrassed me earlier.' / Erin: 'Take it up with the chief of police.'
jokes.setup: Angela approaches Erin to complain about Erin's public meltdown
jokes.punchline: 'Take it up with the chief of police' is a completely unexpected, meaningless response — Erin seems to be using a phrase she's heard without understanding what it means
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Take it up with the chief of police' as a response to a coworker complaint is perfectly wrong — it's a phrase that sort of sounds right but makes absolutely no sense in context. It reveals Erin learned idioms from unusual sources and deploys them confidently. Extremely quotable. The delivery in the show would be completely flat, making it funnier. High character integration — this is distinctly Erin's idiom disorder.

jokes.text: Angela about Andy: 'It's the kind of thing you wish you could have annulled. I want to throw up just thinking about it.' / Erin: 'You are throwing up for the wrong reasons.'
jokes.setup: Angela is dismissing her relationship with Andy as meaningless to her
jokes.punchline: Erin's response — 'You are throwing up for the wrong reasons' — reverses the intended message (Angela is trying to reassure Erin, but Erin interprets Angela's disgust at Andy as a sign something is deeply wrong with him)
jokes.explanation: Erin's misreading of Angela's reassurance as a warning is a good logical inversion. 'Throwing up for the wrong reasons' is a great phrase — weird and specific. Both characters talk past each other in a way that's true to both of them.

jokes.text: Erin: 'You are throwing up for the wrong reasons.'
jokes.setup: Angela says she wants to throw up thinking about Andy; Erin is the wronged party here
jokes.punchline: Erin's flat reassignment of Angela's nausea — the idea that there are 'right' and 'wrong' reasons to throw up, and Angela has the wrong ones
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully economical line — eight words that simultaneously clap back at Angela, acknowledge Erin's own pain, and reveal a surprisingly sharp side of Erin's character. The implied logic ('I should be the one who's sick, not you') is perfectly constructed. Highly quotable. One of Erin's best moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Pam approaches Erin: 'You know, I was engaged before Jim.' / Erin: 'Really?' / Pam: 'Yeah. And he worked here, too.' / Erin: 'It was Andy, wasn't it?'
jokes.setup: Pam tries to comfort Erin by revealing she was also previously engaged to someone at the office
jokes.punchline: Erin immediately assumes it was Andy — the only office romance she currently knows about — which is both logical (from her limited perspective) and absurdly wrong
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is elegant — from Erin's perspective, Andy is the only intra-office romantic she knows about, so her conclusion is perfectly logical and completely wrong. The joke also has a slight meta quality for long-time viewers (Pam and Roy). Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Pam's advice to Erin: 'Sometimes the heart doesn't know what it wants until it finds what it wants.'
jokes.setup: Pam is trying to give Erin meaningful advice about love
jokes.punchline: The advice is a perfectly constructed platitude that means absolutely nothing — it's a tautology dressed up as wisdom, delivered sincerely by Pam who thinks it's helpful
jokes.explanation: The empty platitude is mildly funny but relies entirely on the audience noticing it's a tautology. Not a strong joke — more of a character beat showing Pam's earnest but ineffective counseling style.

jokes.text: Michael discovers the limits of his authority: 'So I can reprimand them, but I can't suspend them? Oh, I can't do either? Uh-huh. Fair enough.'
jokes.setup: Michael calls HR/corporate to confirm his ability to suspend employees
jokes.punchline: He learns he can't suspend, then can't even reprimand — each sentence strips away another piece of his authority until 'Fair enough' accepts his total powerlessness
jokes.explanation: The escalating stripping of authority is well-constructed. 'Fair enough' as the defeated capitulation is perfect — Michael absorbs each blow without complaint. Good payoff to the suspension subplot.

jokes.text: Toby tries to give Michael detailed information: 'I also learned some interesting things about how they structure their...' / Michael: 'Thanks, Toby.'
jokes.setup: Toby helpfully provides legal context after calling Tallahassee for Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael cuts Toby off mid-sentence with a dismissive 'Thanks, Toby' — the abrupt dismissal of someone who actually helped him is both ungrateful and perfectly consistent with their dynamic
jokes.explanation: Michael dismissing Toby is a running gag for the show. The specific beat here — Toby having actually done something useful for once — makes the dismissal slightly more pointed. Functional but reliant on established pattern.

jokes.text: Michael's speech: 'It's not about showing you're in charge or flexing some sort of authority. It's about forgiveness. And, yes, I'm talking about you three in this desk clump right here. I think that if you were to apologize to me, then I would revoke your suspension.'
jokes.setup: Michael gives an inspirational speech about what really matters
jokes.punchline: His universal statement about forgiveness immediately narrows to demanding a personal apology — revealing the speech was self-serving all along
jokes.explanation: The pivot from universal wisdom to personal grievance is a reliable Michael formula — start grand, end petty. The 'desk clump' specificity is a good detail. Competent but familiar territory.

jokes.text: Jim refuses to apologize: 'I really think the only way for me to learn my lesson is to take my suspension.' / Michael: 'Oh, come on. I hope the suspension does that.' / Jim: 'Yeah. Prideful idiots.' [exits]
jokes.setup: Michael offers to revoke the suspensions in exchange for apologies
jokes.punchline: Jim insists he needs the punishment to learn — knowing the suspension is paid time off — and calls himself a 'prideful idiot' as he walks out, happily accepting the vacation
jokes.explanation: Jim's feigned self-flagellation ('prideful idiots') as a cover for gaming a paid day off is a great Jim beat. The straight-faced departure after calling himself a 'prideful idiot' is a nice piece of visual irony.

jokes.text: Gabe's apology: 'Gabriel, I apologize. Great. I kneel before you... Humbly taking your hand upon which I kiss to show my contrition.' / Michael: 'Guys, I would even take a contrite look as an apology.'
jokes.setup: Michael tells the suspended employees to watch how apologies are done, then Gabe demonstrates
jokes.punchline: Gabe's apology is grotesquely theatrical — kneeling and hand-kissing — which both horrifies the room and reveals his complete misreading of social norms to please authority
jokes.explanation: Gabe's servile excess is a great character moment — his desire to ingratiate himself with Michael overcomes all normal social behavior. The kneeling and hand-kissing as a modern office apology is grotesque and funny. Michael's immediate backpedaling ('I would even take a contrite look') confirms even he finds this too much.

jokes.text: Michael, watching Gabe's elaborate apology: 'Guys, I would even take a contrite look as an apology.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is kneeling and kissing hands in his over-the-top apology demonstration.
jokes.punchline: Michael belatedly clarifies that all he wanted was a look.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional about trust, then Erin interrupts: 'Is your name Andy Bernard? What's your real name? Lionel Frankenstein?'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to speak earnestly about trust issues
jokes.punchline: Erin questions whether Andy is even his real name, and her alternative — 'Lionel Frankenstein' — is hilariously specific and bad as a fake name
jokes.explanation: 'Lionel Frankenstein' is the perfect name Erin would invent — it sounds like it was assembled from two unrelated cultural touchstones. The specificity of a name she clearly just made up is very funny. Only Erin would be suspicious enough to question if 'Andy' is real but come up with 'Lionel Frankenstein' as her suspicion.

jokes.text: Andy's confession: 'I mean, yeah, my chest is not naturally hairless, and my parents pay my credit card bill.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to reassure Erin there are no more secrets
jokes.punchline: His 'no more secrets' list includes that he waxes his chest and his parents pay his bills — revealing embarrassing vulnerabilities he's been hiding that are actually worse as character revelations
jokes.explanation: The pairing of 'chest waxing' and 'parents pay credit card' is a perfect two-item list — one vain, one financially pathetic. Both are exactly what Andy would be hiding. Good character specificity.

jokes.text: Erin's breakup speech: 'I think I have to be on my own for a little bit. Like that girl Precious in Precious, Based on the Novel Push by Sapphire. Okay?' / Andy: 'I didn't see that movie.'
jokes.setup: Erin is breaking up with Andy and reaches for a cultural reference to explain her need for independence
jokes.punchline: She invokes the full verbose title of Precious as her touchstone for self-reliance — a callback to her book-on-tape earlier — and Andy's flat 'I didn't see that movie' deflates the entire dramatic moment
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback. Erin's breakup analogy — citing a film about poverty, abuse, and survival as parallel to a minor relationship disclosure — is already absurd. The full verbose title ('Precious, Based on the Novel Push by Sapphire') deployed in a moment of personal drama maximizes the comedy. Andy's utter deflation of the moment with 'I didn't see that movie' is perfect. The structure earned this payoff by setting up the Precious reference earlier. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Michael observes the aftermath: 'That was ugly. I'm sorry that you had to see that.' / Kevin: 'Well, do they still get paid?' / Michael: 'It's tacky to discuss finances.' / Kevin: 'Sounds like they just got to go home with pay.' / Michael: 'Yeah. Pathetic.'
jokes.setup: The office reflects on the dramatic Andy/Erin confrontation and Jim/Pam/Dwight's suspensions
jokes.punchline: Kevin cuts through Michael's faux-dignified framing to get at the practical reality (paid suspension), and Michael's 'Yeah. Pathetic.' agrees with Kevin's assessment while trying to maintain moral high ground
jokes.explanation: Kevin's pragmatic question cuts through Michael's affectations nicely. 'Sounds like they just got to go home with pay' is accurate and delivered with Kevin's signature flat certainty. Michael's agreement ('Yeah. Pathetic') while pretending to disapprove is a good ironic beat.

jokes.text: Kevin does Cookie Monster impression of Michael offering coffee: 'Or cookies!' [said in Cookie Monster voice after Michael offers coffees]
jokes.setup: Michael offers to buy everyone coffees as a peace gesture
jokes.punchline: Kevin can't resist the Cookie Monster opportunity and interjects 'Or cookies!' in the voice
jokes.explanation: A functional running gag beat — Kevin has now fully embraced the impression despite initially protesting it. The brevity is appropriate but it's a predictable joke at this point.

jokes.text: Kevin does extended Michael impression: 'Guys, I'm now going to apologize for the mess that we're in, because corporate told me to. I just want you to know, I laugh like a crazy person.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is now doing an extended Michael impression
jokes.punchline: 'I laugh like a crazy person' as the key detail Kevin chose to immortalize about Michael is both accurate and affectionately cruel
jokes.explanation: Kevin's Michael impression captures something real — Michael does laugh in an unusual way. The corporate-compliance framing is also a good observation about Michael's apologies. Competent impression comedy.

jokes.text: Kevin's Michael impression continues: 'I have to go back to the zoo to the stick insect exhibit.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is continuing his Michael impression
jokes.punchline: The non-sequitur 'stick insect exhibit' as a destination for Michael is random but lands because stick insects are extremely thin — the opposite of Michael — making it a physical comedy dig
jokes.explanation: The stick insect reference is mildly absurdist. The implicit physical comparison is there if you look for it, but it's not a tight enough joke to be a standout. It's a competent weird flourish.

jokes.text: Kevin's Michael impression: 'Ciao. Right? Ciao. I say ciao 'cause I'm fancy from Tallahassee.' / Gabe: 'Why don't we say ciao to the impressions? / [beat] / Ciao.'
jokes.setup: Kevin's impression mocks Michael for saying 'ciao' and attributing it to being 'fancy from Tallahassee'
jokes.punchline: Gabe attempts to shut down the impressions with a 'ciao' pun ('say ciao to the impressions') — which is a weak dad joke — and then says 'Ciao' again, apparently ending things while also doing the thing Kevin was mocking
jokes.explanation: 'Fancy from Tallahassee' is a good anti-prestige descriptor — Tallahassee being the antithesis of cosmopolitan sophistication. Gabe's 'ciao' pun is a weak but charming dad-joke attempt. The meta-irony of Gabe saying 'ciao' to end impressions is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Someone mutters 'Stick insect.' after Gabe walks away, and someone else says 'God.'
jokes.setup: Gabe has just tried and failed to shut down the impressions
jokes.punchline: The immediate callback to 'stick insect' after his exit, followed by 'God' — one confirming the joke, one expressing disbelief at Gabe's situation
jokes.explanation: A quick button joke — the murmured 'Stick insect' is a tag on the running gag, effective but not adding much beyond keeping the image fresh in the room.

jokes.text: Erin alone watching Cookie Monster video, Michael finds her: 'Sorry. I thought everyone was gone.' / Michael: 'No, no. I was just watching Cookie Monster. It finally downloaded.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just delivered a heartfelt apology to Erin about ruining her Secretary's Day
jokes.punchline: His reason for still being in the office is that he was waiting for the Cookie Monster video to download — his emotional consolation moment is revealed to have been incidental to a personal errand
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Michael was only there for the Cookie Monster download is a good callback payoff and consistent with joke #53. His priorities have been consistent throughout — the human moment he creates is accidental.

jokes.text: Michael comforts Erin by dismissing Angela: 'She doesn't hold a candle to you, Erin. She's old enough to be your mom, for one thing, and she's, like, three feet tall, and she wears pioneer women clothing, and I don't think she's ever pooped in her life.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to make Erin feel better about Andy's past with Angela
jokes.punchline: His 'reassurances' are a list of escalating Angela insults — each stranger than the last — culminating in 'I don't think she's ever pooped in her life,' which is both an insult and somehow a backhanded compliment depending on interpretation
jokes.explanation: This is a great escalation sequence. 'Pioneer women clothing' is specific and accurate to Angela. 'She's never pooped in her life' is the absurdist peak — it sounds like an insult but it's unclear whether it IS one, and the uncertainty makes it funnier. Michael's attempt at comfort through escalating disparagement is perfectly in character. The list structure builds well. High quotability — 'pioneer women clothing' and 'never pooped in her life' are both memorable.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Andy? You know... Come on. Andy, his butt looks big in those khakis.' / Erin: 'Oh, I like his butt.' / Michael: 'You said butt.' / Erin: 'You tricked me.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to make Erin feel better by insulting Andy
jokes.punchline: Erin's defensive 'I like his butt' reveals she's still attached; Michael's childlike 'You said butt' treats it as a game-winning gotcha; Erin's 'You tricked me' accepts the framing
jokes.explanation: This exchange is beautifully structured. Michael's butt insult gets Erin to defend Andy, Michael's 'You said butt' treats the whole thing as a childish word game, and Erin's 'You tricked me' fully accepts that frame — implying she thinks Michael did it deliberately as therapy. The three-beat exchange works perfectly, each line escalating the absurdity while also revealing real emotional warmth between Michael and Erin. Both characters are completely in character throughout. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Erin: 'Oh, I like his butt.' Michael: 'You said butt.' Erin: 'You tricked me.'
jokes.setup: Michael makes a butt comment about Andy; Erin instinctively defends Andy's butt
jokes.punchline: Michael celebrates 'You said butt' — and Erin's 'You tricked me' implies Michael has accomplished his secret goal of getting her to think fondly of Andy
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in economy. 'You said butt' / 'You tricked me' is a perfect three-beat joke that also reveals Michael has been running a covert reconciliation play — which is surprisingly emotionally intelligent for Michael Scott. The comedy and the sweetness balance beautifully. 'You tricked me' implies Michael's entire Angela-insult speech was a scheme to get Erin to think about Andy's butt, which recontextualizes the whole scene. Highly quotable and carries strong emotional resonance.

jokes.text: Michael attempts to tell Erin about his neighbor Tom Dizemore: 'You'd love... This... This guy in my neighborhood, Tom Dizemore. This is him. "Hey! Hey, Scott..."' [trails off or is cut off]
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to connect with Erin and pivots to telling a neighborhood anecdote
jokes.punchline: The story about Tom Dizemore appears to go nowhere — Michael does an impression ('Hey! Hey, Scott...') but we never get the punchline, and the joke is in the aborted anecdote itself
jokes.explanation: The incomplete anecdote is a recognizable comedy format — a joke that's funny because it never arrives. However, without the full transcript confirming what happened (the story seems genuinely interrupted), it's hard to assess fully. Likely a minor beat that serves the scene's rhythm.

jokes.text: Confessional coda: 'Sometimes telling someone something is hard.' / Then cut to: 'Well, at least somebody made her happy on Secretary's Day.'
jokes.setup: Michael reflects philosophically on the events of the day
jokes.punchline: The valedictory 'at least somebody made her happy on Secretary's Day' coming after Michael himself caused much of her distress is an ironic self-congratulation — but delivered in Michael's genuinely warm register so it lands as both joke and sweet moment
jokes.explanation: A nice thematic button on the episode. Michael's obliviousness to his own role in the day's disasters allows him genuine warmth at the end. The irony is gentle rather than sharp. Works better emotionally than as a pure comedy beat.

jokes.text: Kevin's Oscar/Count retaliation video: Oscar calls Kevin about accounting discrepancies; Kevin reveals he made a Cookie Monster vs. The Count parody with Oscar as The Count because 'the Count is purple, and Oscar wears purple.'
jokes.setup: Kevin made a retaliatory video mocking Oscar using The Count from Sesame Street
jokes.punchline: Kevin's reasoning — Oscar wears purple, The Count is purple — is a logic chain that sounds coherent but ignores the obvious choice (Oscar the Grouch), which others immediately point out
jokes.explanation: The joke is multi-layered: (1) Kevin missed the obvious Oscar the Grouch connection (Oscar = Grouch) and chose The Count instead based on clothing color; (2) his reasoning is internally coherent but misses the joke everyone else would make; (3) 'Why didn't you do Oscar the Grouch?' is a perfect straight-man observation. Kevin's logic being plausible but wrong is classic Kevin comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight evaluates the video: 'Nailed him. Nailed him! Good work, Cookie Monster.'
jokes.setup: The office watches Kevin's Count/Oscar parody video
jokes.punchline: Dwight's enthusiastic assessment ('Nailed him. Nailed him!') followed by addressing Kevin as 'Cookie Monster' — the nickname has now permanently stuck — is both a running gag payoff and Dwight being unexpectedly supportive
jokes.explanation: A good episode-closing beat for the Cookie Monster subplot. 'Good work, Cookie Monster' is a warm, absurd sendoff for the bit. Dwight calling Kevin by the nickname without irony is funny but not a major joke.

tmdb_overview: Michael gets kicked out of the bar when he pulls out all the stops to impress a friend of Jim and Pam's. Meanwhile, Andy and Erin do their best to keep their relationship under wraps. Dwight rethinks his pre-natal contract with Angela.
